Floor, ceiling and the space between

Árpád Bényi Address: Department of Mathematics, Western Washington University
516 High Street, Bellingham, Washington 98225, USA Email address: Arpad.Benyi@wwu.edu and Branko Ćurgus Address: Department of Mathematics, Western Washington University
516 High Street, Bellingham, Washington 98225, USA Email address: Branko.Curgus@wwu.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

Motivated by a question on the ranges of the commutators of dilated floor functions in [9], together with a related problem in [3], we investigate the precise ranges of certain generalized polynomials dependent on a real parameter. Our analysis requires non-trivial tools, including Kronecker’s approximation theorem. The results highlight sharp distinctions between irrational parameters and sub-unitary and supra-unitary rational parameters. We also propose several conjectures for the irrational and supra-unitary rational cases, supported by extensive computations in Wolfram Mathematica.

Key words and phrases: 
mod operator, Bézout’s identity, Kronecker’s approximation theorem
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11A99, 11J54; Secondary 26A09, 26D07

1. Introduction

Given a real number xx, the floor and ceiling of xx are defined respectively by

⌊x⌋:=max⁡{m∈ℤ:m≤x}and⌈x⌉:=min⁡{n∈ℤ:n≥x}.\lfloor x\rfloor:=\max\bigl\{m\in\mathbb{Z}:m\leq x\bigr\}\quad\text{and}\quad\lceil x\rceil:=\min\bigl\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:n\geq x\bigr\}.

Equivalently, ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor and ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil are the unique integers satisfying

⌊x⌋≤x<⌊x⌋+1and⌈x⌉−1<x≤⌈x⌉.\lfloor x\rfloor\leq x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\quad\text{and}\quad\lceil x\rceil-1<x\leq\lceil x\rceil. (1.1)

It is also clear from the definitions that ⌈x⌉−⌊x⌋∈{0,1}\lceil x\rceil-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\{0,1\}, and that ⌈x⌉−⌊x⌋=0\lceil x\rceil-\lfloor x\rfloor=0 if and only if x∈ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}.

The definitions and names of the floor and ceiling functions were introduced by Iverson in the context of computer science [7, p. 12]; see also [6, Chapter 3] for additional history and properties. Despite their elementary definitions, these functions arise in a wide range of applications. For instance, they appear in the statement of the Quadratic Reciprocity Law, in Legendre’s formula for the exponent of the highest power of a prime dividing a given integer, and in expressions involving the Riemann zeta function, among many others.

The investigation of digital straight lines, that is, drawing lines on a computer screen, naturally leads to dilated floor functions and their commutators. For α∈ℝ∖{0}\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}, define the following functions:

ℓα\displaystyle\ell_{\alpha} :ℝ→ℝ,\displaystyle:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, ℓα​(x)\displaystyle\qquad\ell_{\alpha}(x) =α​x,\displaystyle=\alpha x,
gα\displaystyle g_{\alpha} :ℝ→ℤ,\displaystyle:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{Z}, gα​(x)\displaystyle\qquad g_{\alpha}(x) =⌊α​x⌋.\displaystyle=\lfloor\alpha x\rfloor.

From this perspective, gαg_{\alpha} discretizes ℓα\ell_{\alpha} at the length scale 1/α1/\alpha, in the sense that the difference ℓα−gα\ell_{\alpha}-g_{\alpha} is a bounded function. Understanding the interaction of the discretizations at two different scales α\alpha and β\beta is mathematically equivalent to the study of the commutator of the functions gαg_{\alpha} and gβg_{\beta} defined by

[gα,gβ]=gα∘gβ−gβ∘gα.[g_{\alpha},g_{\beta}]=g_{\alpha}\circ g_{\beta}-g_{\beta}\circ g_{\alpha}.

While the commutator [ℓα,ℓβ][\ell_{\alpha},\ell_{\beta}] vanishes identically, the authors in [9] highlight how “discretization generally destroys such commutativity,” underscoring the new complexity introduced by the floor functions. Their main result characterizes all pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) for which the range of the commutator [gα,gβ][g_{\alpha},g_{\beta}] is precisely {0}\{0\}; see also [8]. Subsequent work in [10, 11] extended this analysis by asking when the range of the commutator is contained in [0,∞)[0,\infty), drawing on tools such as Beatty sequences, Lie groups, and the Sylvester duality theorem. With the exception of [9], however, none of these studies addressed the problem of determining the precise range of commutators.

In light of this background, it is natural to consider the simplest case where the dilation parameters coincide. Both gα2g_{\alpha^{2}} and gα∘gαg_{\alpha}\circ g_{\alpha} are step-function approximations of ℓα2\ell_{\alpha^{2}}. Thus, in place of the trivial commutator [gα,gα]=0[g_{\alpha},g_{\alpha}]=0, one may study the difference

gα2−gα∘gα,g_{\alpha^{2}}-g_{\alpha}\circ g_{\alpha},

which defines a so-called generalized polynomial in the sense of [1].

Specifically, for α>0\alpha>0, define the function fα:ℕ→ℤf_{\alpha}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z} by

fα​(n)=gα2​(n)−gα​(gα​(n))=⌊α2​n⌋−⌊α⁡⌊α​n⌋⌋,∀n∈ℕ.f_{\alpha}(n)=g_{\alpha^{2}}(n)-g_{\alpha}\bigl(g_{\alpha}(n)\bigr)=\bigl\lfloor\alpha^{2}\,n\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor\alpha\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor,\quad\forall\,n\in\mathbb{N}. (1.2)

An instance of this function already appeared in a problem posed for high school students [3], which asked for the precise range of fτf_{\tau}, with τ=(1+2017)/2\tau=\bigl(1+\sqrt{2017}\bigr)/2.

In this note, we shall investigate a generalization of the problem in [3] and discover some nice connections with other number theoretical facts, such as the concept of modulo (or simply, mod) operator [12] or Kronecker’s approximation theorem [2, Chapter III]; see also [13] and [14]. We also state several conjectures regarding the precise range of fαf_{\alpha} for general supra-unitary rational parameters, and also for irrational parameters α\alpha. Some of the questions that arise are naturally related to the size of the space between appropriate floor and ceiling functions; see, for example, Remark 3.1 and Remark  4.1.

Range⁡(fα):={fα​(n):n∈ℕ}.\Range(f_{\alpha}):=\bigl\{f_{\alpha}(n):n\in\mathbb{N}\bigr\}.

It is clear that for α∈ℕ\alpha\in\mathbb{N} we have a trivial range, Range⁡(fα)={0}.\Range(f_{\alpha})=\{0\}. Therefore, for the remainder of our discussion we will assume that α>0\alpha>0 and α∉ℕ\alpha\not\in\mathbb{N}.

Lemma 3.1.

n=b2q+r,r∈\llbracket0,b2−1\rrbracket.n=b^{2}q+r,\quad r\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b^{2}-1\bigr\rrbracket.

Now, if r=0r=0, it is easy to see that fα​(b2​q)=0f_{\alpha}(b^{2}q)=0. If r≠0r\neq 0, then

fα​(n)\displaystyle f_{\alpha}(n) =⌊a2​q+r​a2b2⌋−⌊ab​⌊a​b​q+a​rb⌋⌋\displaystyle=\bigg\lfloor a^{2}q+\frac{ra^{2}}{b^{2}}\bigg\rfloor-\bigg\lfloor\frac{a}{b}\left\lfloor abq+\frac{ar}{b}\right\rfloor\bigg\rfloor
=a2​q+⌊r​a2b2⌋−a2​q−⌊ab​⌊a​rb⌋⌋\displaystyle=a^{2}q+\bigg\lfloor\frac{ra^{2}}{b^{2}}\bigg\rfloor-a^{2}q-\bigg\lfloor\frac{a}{b}\left\lfloor\frac{ar}{b}\right\rfloor\bigg\rfloor
=fα​(r).∎\displaystyle=f_{\alpha}(r).\qed

and

ϕa,b​(x​r)=x​r​a−y​r​b=r⁡(x​a−y​b)=r.∎\phi_{a,b}\mkern-1.0mu(xr)=xra-yrb=r(xa-yb)=r.\qed

which is strictly greater than b2−1b^{2}-1, it is not possible that \llbracket​0,b2−1​\rrbracket\bigl\llbracket 0,b^{2}-1\bigr\rrbracket is a subset of the range. In particular, then 11 is not in the range of the function defined in (3.1). This proves the claim. ∎

⌊α2​n⌋−⌊α⁡⌊α​n⌋⌋={0ifnis even,s+⌊n4⌋−⌊n+14⌋ifnis odd.\lfloor\alpha^{2}n\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor\alpha\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor=\begin{cases}0&\text{if}\quad n\quad\text{is even},\\[7.0pt] s+\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n}{4}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n+1}{4}\Big\rfloor&\text{if}\quad n\quad\text{is odd}.\end{cases}

Note now that ⌊n4⌋−⌊n+14⌋=−1\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n}{4}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n+1}{4}\Big\rfloor=-1 for nn odd such that n≡3n\equiv 3 (mod 4), while ⌊n4⌋−⌊n+14⌋=0\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n}{4}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\dfrac{n+1}{4}\Big\rfloor=0 for n≢3n\not\equiv 3 (mod 4). This implies that

Range⁡(f2​s−1+12)={0,s−1,s}.∎\Range\bigl(f_{2s-1+\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)=\{0,s-1,s\}.\qed

In what follows, we explore the general situation in which the (non-integer) rational number α>1\alpha>1 has denominator b∈ℕ∖{1}.b\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}. By the division algorithm, we can express our parameter as

α=(s​b+u)+ab,\alpha=(sb+u)+\frac{a}{b},

where s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket and a∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketa\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. We have the following decomposition of fαf_{\alpha}.

Proposition 3.6.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}, s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket and a∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketa\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. Then

fs​b+u+ab=s​ϕa,b+fu+ab,f_{sb+u+\frac{a}{b}}=s\mkern 1.0mu\phi_{a,b}+f_{u+\frac{a}{b}},

where ϕa,b\phi_{a,b} is the function defined in Proposition 3.2.

Proof.

Straightforward calculations give that, for α=(s​b+u)+ab,\alpha=(sb+u)+\frac{a}{b}, we have

⌊α2​n⌋\displaystyle\lfloor\alpha^{2}n\rfloor =(s​b+u)2​n+2​a​s​n+⌊2​a​ub​n+a2b2​n⌋\displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+2asn+\Big\lfloor\frac{2au}{b}n+\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}n\Big\rfloor
=(s​b+u)2​n+2​a​s​n−u2​n+⌊(ab+u)2​n⌋.\displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+2asn-u^{2}n+\Big\lfloor\mkern-3.0mu\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)^{2}n\mkern-1.0mu\Big\rfloor.

Next, we have

α​⌊α​n⌋\displaystyle\alpha\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor =(s​b+u)2​n+a​s​n+s​b​⌊ab​n⌋+a​ub​n+(ab+u)​⌊ab​n⌋\displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+asn+sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor+\frac{au}{b}n+\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor
=(s​b+u)2​n+a​s​n+s​b​⌊ab​n⌋+2​a​ub​n+a2b2​n−(ab+u)​         ab​n         \displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+asn+sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor+\frac{2au}{b}n+\frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}n-\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\mathopen{\vbox{\hbox{\makebox[0.0pt][l]{\rotatebox[origin={l}]{70.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}\rotatebox[origin={l}]{-70.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}}}\frac{a}{b}n\mkern-1.0mu\mathclose{\vbox{\hbox{\makebox[0.0pt][l]{\rotatebox[origin={l}]{110.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}\rotatebox[origin={l}]{250.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}}}
=(s​b+u)2​n+a​s​n+s​b​⌊ab​n⌋−u2​n\displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+asn+sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor-u^{2}n
+(ab+u)2​n−(ab+u)​         (ab+u)​n         \displaystyle\mkern 140.0mu+\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)^{2}n-\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\mathopen{\vbox{\hbox{\makebox[0.0pt][l]{\rotatebox[origin={l}]{70.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}\rotatebox[origin={l}]{-70.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}}}\mkern-1.0mu\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)n\mkern-1.0mu\mathclose{\vbox{\hbox{\makebox[0.0pt][l]{\rotatebox[origin={l}]{110.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}\rotatebox[origin={l}]{250.0}{\rule{10.76385pt}{0.55pt}}}}}
=(s​b+u)2​n+a​s​n+s​b​⌊ab​n⌋−u2​n+(ab+u)​⌊(ab+u)​n⌋.\displaystyle=(sb+u)^{2}n+asn+sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor-u^{2}n+\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\Big\lfloor\mkern-3.0mu\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)n\mkern-1.0mu\Big\rfloor.

Thus,

⌊α⁡⌊α​n⌋⌋=(s​b+u)2​n+a​s​n+s​b​⌊ab​n⌋−u2​n+⌊(ab+u)​⌊(ab+u)​n⌋⌋\bigl\lfloor\alpha\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor=(sb+u)^{2}n+asn+sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor-u^{2}n+\bigg\lfloor\mkern-5.0mu\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\Big\lfloor\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)n\Big\rfloor\bigg\rfloor

and

fα​(n)\displaystyle f_{\alpha}(n) =a​s​n−s​b​⌊ab​n⌋+⌊(ab+u)2​n⌋−⌊(ab+u)​⌊(ab+u)​n⌋⌋\displaystyle=asn-sb\Big\lfloor\frac{a}{b}n\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)^{2}n\Big\rfloor-\bigg\lfloor\mkern-3.0mu\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)\Big\lfloor\left(\frac{a}{b}+u\right)n\Big\rfloor\bigg\rfloor
=s​ϕa,b​(n)+fu+ab​(n).∎\displaystyle=s\mkern 1.0mu\phi_{a,b}(n)+f_{u+\frac{a}{b}}(n).\qed

Two immediate consequences of the decomposition in Proposition 3.6 are the following.

Corollary 3.7.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}, s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket and a∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketa\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket relatively prime to bb. Then

Range⁡(fs​b+u+ab)⊆s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket+\llbracket​0,u+1​\rrbracket.\Range\bigl(f_{sb+u+\frac{a}{b}}\bigr)\subseteq s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket+\bigl\llbracket 0,u+1\bigr\rrbracket.
Proof.

Noting that ⌈u+ab⌉=u+1\Big\lceil u+\frac{a}{b}\Big\rceil=u+1, the inclusion follows from Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 2.1 ∎

Corollary 3.8.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\} and s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}. Then

Range⁡(fs​b+1b)=s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket.\Range\bigl(f_{sb+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket.
Proof.

By Proposition 3.6 and Proposition 3.4, part (i), for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have

fs​b+1b​(n)=s​ϕ1,b​(n)+f1b​(n)=s​ϕ1,b​(n).f_{sb+\frac{1}{b}}(n)=s\phi_{1,b}(n)+f_{\frac{1}{b}}(n)=s\phi_{1,b}(n).

The equality Range⁡(fs​b+1b)=s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket\Range\bigl(f_{sb+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket now follows from Proposition 3.2. ∎

While Proposition 3.6 provides a good starting point for identifying the exact range of functions such as fs​b+1bf_{sb+\frac{1}{b}}, we need a slightly modified version of it to deal with other supra-unitary parameters of the form s​b+u+1bsb+u+\frac{1}{b} with u>0u>0.

Lemma 3.9.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}, s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, and u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. Let n=b​t+rn=bt+r with t,r∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett,r\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. Then

fs​b+u+1b​(n)=s​r+⌊2​u​rb+tb+rb2⌋−⌊u​rb+tb⌋.f_{sb+u+\frac{1}{b}}(n)=sr+\Big\lfloor\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor.

In particular, for u=0u=0, we obtain fs​b+1b​(n)=s​r,f_{sb+\frac{1}{b}}(n)=sr, which implies the statement of Corollary 3.8.

Proof.

The calculations are similar to the ones in the proof of Proposition 3.6. We only present the essential identities. With α=b​s+u+1b\alpha=bs+u+\frac{1}{b}, we have

⌊α2​n⌋=(b​s+u)2​n+2​s​n+2​u​t+⌊2​u​rb+tb+rb2⌋\lfloor\alpha^{2}n\rfloor=(bs+u)^{2}n+2sn+2ut+\Big\lfloor\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor

and

⌊α⁡⌊α​n⌋⌋=(b​s+u)2​n+s​n+b​s​t+2​u​t+⌊u​rb+tb⌋.\bigl\lfloor\alpha\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor=(bs+u)^{2}n+sn+bst+2ut+\Big\lfloor\frac{ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor.

Therefore,

fα​(n)\displaystyle f_{\alpha}(n) =s⁡(n−b​t)+⌊2​u​rb+tb+rb2⌋−⌊u​rb+tb⌋\displaystyle=s(n-bt)+\Big\lfloor\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor
=s​r+⌊2​u​rb+tb+rb2⌋−⌊u​rb+tb⌋.∎\displaystyle=sr+\Big\lfloor\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{ur}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor.\qed

Our next result states an inclusion relation that improves the inclusion stated in Corollary 3.7 when a=1a=1.

Proposition 3.10.

For all b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\}, all s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, and all u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket such that s​b+u∈ℕsb+u\in\mathbb{N}, we have

Range⁡(fs​b+u+1b)⊆s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket+\llbracket​0,u​\rrbracket.\Range\bigl(f_{sb+u+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)\subseteq s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket+\bigl\llbracket 0,u\bigr\rrbracket.
Proof.

Let α=s​b+u+1b\alpha=sb+u+\frac{1}{b}. Using the notation from Lemma 3.9, with n=b​t+rn=bt+r and t,r∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket,t,r\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, we can rewrite

fα​(n)=s​r+⌊2​u​rb+nb2⌋−⌊(u​b−1)​rb2+nb2⌋.f_{\alpha}(n)=sr+\Big\lfloor\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{(ub-1)r}{b^{2}}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor. (3.6)

Let us denote for simplicity

x⁡(n,u)=2​u​rb+nb2​and​y​(n,u)=(u​b−1)​rb2+nb2.x(n,u)=\frac{2ur}{b}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}\,\,\text{and}\,\,y(n,u)=\frac{(ub-1)r}{b^{2}}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}.

Clearly, if u=0u=0, we have ⌊x⁡(n,u)⌋=⌊y⁡(n,u)⌋=0.\lfloor x(n,u)\rfloor=\lfloor y(n,u)\rfloor=0. If u≥1u\geq 1, we see that

x⁡(n,u)−y⁡(n,u)=(u​b+1)​rb2≥0x(n,u)-y(n,u)=\frac{(ub+1)r}{b^{2}}\geq 0

and

x⁡(n,u)−y⁡(n,u)≤(u​b+1)​(b−1)b2=u−u−1b−1b2<u.x(n,u)-y(n,u)\leq\frac{(ub+1)(b-1)}{b^{2}}=u-\frac{u-1}{b}-\frac{1}{b^{2}}<u.

Therefore,

0≤⌊x⁡(n,u)−y⁡(n,u)⌋≤⌊x⁡(n,u)⌋−⌊y⁡(n,u)⌋,0\leq\bigl\lfloor x(n,u)-y(n,u)\bigr\rfloor\leq\bigl\lfloor x(n,u)\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor y(n,u)\bigr\rfloor,

and

⌊x⁡(n,u)⌋−⌊y⁡(n,u)⌋≤⌊x⁡(n,u)−y⁡(n,u)⌋+1≤(u−1)+1=u.\bigl\lfloor x(n,u)\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor y(n,u)\bigr\rfloor\leq\lfloor x(n,u)-y(n,u)\rfloor+1\leq(u-1)+1=u.

In other words, for all n∈\llbracket​0,b2−1​\rrbracketn\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b^{2}-1\bigr\rrbracket and u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, we have

⌊x⁡(n,u)⌋−⌊y⁡(n,u)⌋∈\llbracket​0,u​\rrbracket.\bigl\lfloor x(n,u)\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor y(n,u)\bigr\rfloor\in\bigl\llbracket 0,u\bigr\rrbracket.

This finishes the proof. ∎

In particular, when u=1u=1, we get the following.

Corollary 3.11.

For all b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\} and all s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} we have

Range⁡(fs​b+1+1b)⊆s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket+\llbracket​0,1​\rrbracket.\Range\bigl(f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)\subseteq s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket+\bigl\llbracket 0,1\bigr\rrbracket.
Corollary 3.12.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\}. Then

Range⁡(f1+1b)={0,1}.\Range\bigl(f_{1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=\{0,1\}.
Proof.

Using Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 3.11, we only need to prove that 1∈Range⁡(f1+1b).1\in\Range\bigl(f_{1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr). We claim that f1+1b​(b−1)=1.f_{1+\frac{1}{b}}(b-1)=1. Indeed, letting s=0s=0, u=1u=1, t=0t=0 and r=b−1r=b-1 in Lemma 3.9 (or, alternately, in the formula (3.6)), we have

f1+1b​(b−1)=⌊2−b+1b2⌋−⌊b−1b⌋.f_{1+\frac{1}{b}}(b-1)=\Big\lfloor 2-\frac{b+1}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{b-1}{b}\Big\rfloor.

But since 1<2−b+1b2<21<2-\frac{b+1}{b^{2}}<2 and 0<b−1b<10<\frac{b-1}{b}<1, we get f1+1b​(b−1)=1.f_{1+\frac{1}{b}}(b-1)=1. ∎

A refinement of the argument in Corollary 3.12 gives the next result.

Corollary 3.13.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\}. Then

Range⁡(fb+1+1b)=\llbracket​0,b​\rrbracket.\Range\bigl(f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=\bigl\llbracket 0,b\bigr\rrbracket.
Proof.

Using again Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 3.11, it suffices to show that \llbracket​1,b​\rrbracket⊆Range⁡(fb+1+1b).\bigl\llbracket 1,b\bigr\rrbracket\subseteq\Range\bigl(f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr). We proceed in two steps. First, we claim that fb+1+1b​(b2−b+1)=1f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}(b^{2}-b+1)=1. Indeed, letting s=1s=1, u=1u=1, t=b−1t=b-1 and r=1r=1 in Lemma 3.9, and since 1<1+b+1b2<21<1+\frac{b+1}{b^{2}}<2, we get

fb+1+1b​(b2−b+1)=1+⌊1+b+1b2⌋−1=1.f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigl(b^{2}-b+1\bigr)=1+\Big\lfloor 1+\frac{b+1}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-1=1.

Secondly, let us fix r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. We will show that there exists a t⁡(r)∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett(r)\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket such that fb+1+1b​(b​t​(r)+r)=r+1f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigl(bt(r)+r\bigr)=r+1. Indeed, let s=u=1s=u=1 and t=t⁡(r):=b−1−rt=t(r):=b-1-r in Lemma 3.9 and notice that

fb+1+1b​(b​t+r)=r+⌊rb+rb2+b−1b⌋−⌊b−1b⌋=r+⌊1+r−1b+rb2⌋.f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigl(bt+r\bigr)=r+\Big\lfloor\mkern-1.0mu\frac{r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{b-1}{b}\mkern-1.0mu\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\mkern-1.0mu\frac{b-1}{b}\mkern-1.0mu\Big\rfloor=r+\Big\lfloor\mkern-1.0mu1+\frac{r-1}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}\mkern-1.0mu\Big\rfloor.

Next, observe that 0<r−1b+rb2<10<\frac{r-1}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}<1. The left-side inequality is trivial while the right-side inequality is equivalent to (r−1)​b+r<b2⇔r<b(r-1)b+r<b^{2}\Leftrightarrow r<b. This proves the claim fb+1+1b​(b⁡(b−1−r)+r)=r+1f_{b+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigl(b(b-1-r)+r\bigr)=r+1 and concludes our proof. ∎

The following corollary generalizes Corollaries 3.12 and 3.13.

Corollary 3.14.

For all b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-2.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\} and s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} we have

Range⁡(fs​b+1+1b)=(s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket)∪(s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket+{1}).\Range\bigl(f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket\bigr)\cup\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket+\{1\}\bigr).
Proof.

It is sufficient to consider s>1s>1. By Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 3.11, it suffices to show that 1∉Range⁡(fs​b+1+1b)1\not\in\Range\bigl(f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr) and s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket+{0,1}⊆Range⁡(fs​b+1+1b)s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket+\{0,1\}\subseteq\Range\bigl(f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr). First of all, using the notation from Lemma 3.9, for all r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, we have fs​b+1+1b​(b​t+r)≥s​r≥s>1f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}(bt+r)\geq sr\geq s>1 (and, as we have seen before, fs​b+1+1b​(b​t)=0f_{sb+1+\frac{1}{b}}(bt)=0). For the second claim, we will show that for fixed r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, we can find t0​(r),t1​(r)∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett_{0}(r),t_{1}(r)\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket such that

fα​(b​t0​(r)+r)=s​randfα​(b​t1​(r)+r)=s​r+1.f_{\alpha}\bigl(bt_{0}(r)+r\bigr)=sr\quad\text{and}\quad f_{\alpha}\bigl(bt_{1}(r)+r\bigr)=sr+1.

Equivalently, we want to show that, for fixed r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, the equations

⌊2​rb+rb2+tb⌋=⌊rb+tb⌋,\Big\lfloor\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor=\Big\lfloor\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor, (3.7)

respectively

⌊2​rb+rb2+tb⌋=⌈rb+tb⌉\Big\lfloor\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor=\Big\lceil\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rceil (3.8)

are solvable in t∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket.

The equation  (3.7) has the solution t0=t0​(r)=b−rt_{0}=t_{0}(r)=b-r. Indeed, ⌊rb+t0b⌋=1\displaystyle\Big\lfloor\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t_{0}}{b}\Big\rfloor=1 and

2​rb+rb2+t0b=rb+rb2+1∈(1,2)\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t_{0}}{b}=\frac{r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+1\in(1,2)

since r≤b−1<b2b+1r\leq b-1<\displaystyle\frac{b^{2}}{b+1}, therefore also ⌊2​rb+rb2+t0b⌋=1\displaystyle\Big\lfloor\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t_{0}}{b}\Big\rfloor=1. The equation  (3.8) has the solution t1​(r)=b−1−rt_{1}(r)=b-1-r by the argument proving Corollary 3.13. ∎

Similar considerations to the ones proving Proposition 3.10 and Corollary 3.14 give the following result.

Corollary 3.15.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-3.0mu\setminus\mkern-3.0mu\{1\} and s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}. Then

Range⁡(fs​b−1+1b)=(s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket)∪(s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket−{1}).\Range\bigl(f_{sb-1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)=\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket\bigr)\cup\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket-\{1\}\bigr).
Proof.

Let α=s​b−1+1b=(s−1)​b+(b−1)+1b\alpha=sb-1+\frac{1}{b}=(s-1)b+(b-1)+\frac{1}{b}. With ss replaced by s−1∈ℕ∪{0}s-1\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, and u=b−1u=b-1, in the proof of Proposition 3.10, we find that (3.6) can be rewritten as

fα​(n)=(s−1)​r+⌊2​(b−1)​rb+nb2⌋−⌊((b−1)​b−1)​rb2+nb2⌋.f_{\alpha}(n)=(s-1)r+\Big\lfloor\frac{2(b-1)r}{b}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{((b-1)b-1)r}{b^{2}}+\frac{n}{b^{2}}\Big\rfloor.

As before, letting now n=b​t+rn=bt+r with t,r∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket,t,r\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, a few simple manipulations yield

fα​(b​t+r)=s​r−(⌊rb+tb⌋−⌊−2​rb+rb2+tb⌋).f_{\alpha}(bt+r)=sr-\Bigl(\Big\lfloor\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor-\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor\Bigr). (3.9)

Denote

x⁡(b,t,r)=rb+tb​and​y​(b,t,r)=−2​rb+rb2+tb.x(b,t,r)=\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\,\,\text{and}\,\,y(b,t,r)=-\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}.

We have

x⁡(b,t,r)−y⁡(b,t,r)=(b−1)​rb2∈(0,(b−1)2b2]⊆(0,1).x(b,t,r)-y(b,t,r)=\frac{(b-1)r}{b^{2}}\in\Bigl(0,\frac{(b-1)^{2}}{b^{2}}\Bigr]\subseteq(0,1).

This implies that ⌊x⁡(b,t,r)−y⁡(b,t,r)⌋=0\bigl\lfloor x(b,t,r)-y(b,t,r)\bigr\rfloor=0, thus

⌊x⁡(b,t,r)⌋−⌊y⁡(b,t,r)⌋∈{0,1}.\bigl\lfloor x(b,t,r)\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor y(b,t,r)\bigr\rfloor\in\{0,1\}. (3.10)

Using (3.9) and (3.10), we conclude that

Range⁡(fs​b−1+1b)⊆s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket−{0,1}.\Range\bigl(f_{sb-1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)\subseteq s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket-\{0,1\}.

Since −1∉Range⁡(fs​b−1+1b)-1\not\in\Range\bigl(f_{sb-1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr), we have

Range⁡(fs​b−1+1b)⊆(s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket)∪(s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket−{1}).\Range\bigl(f_{sb-1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr)\subseteq\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket\bigr)\cup\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket-\{1\}\bigr).

For the converse inclusion, as in the proof of Corollary 3.14, it suffices to show that

s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket−{0,1}⊆Range⁡(fs​b−1+1b),s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket-\{0,1\}\subseteq\Range\bigl(f_{sb-1+\frac{1}{b}}\bigr),

which is equivalent to showing that for fixed r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, we can find t⁡(r),t~​(r)∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett(r),\tilde{t}(r)\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket such that

fα​(b​t​(r)+r)=s​randfα​(b​t~​(r)+r)=s​r−1.f_{\alpha}\bigl(bt(r)+r\bigr)=sr\quad\text{and}\quad f_{\alpha}\bigl(b\tilde{t}(r)+r\bigr)=sr-1.

Equivalently, we want to show that, for fixed r∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketr\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket, the equations

⌊−rb+tb⌋=⌊−2​rb+rb2+tb⌋,\Big\lfloor\mkern-4.0mu-\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor=\Big\lfloor\mkern-4.0mu-\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor, (3.11)

respectively

⌊−rb+tb⌋=1+⌊−2​rb+rb2+tb⌋\Big\lfloor\mkern-4.0mu-\frac{r}{b}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor=1+\Big\lfloor\mkern-4.0mu-\frac{2r}{b}+\frac{r}{b^{2}}+\frac{t}{b}\Big\rfloor (3.12)

are solvable in t∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. The equation (3.11) has the solution t⁡(r)=r−1t(r)=r-1. The equation (3.12) has the solution t~​(r)=r\tilde{t}(r)=r. ∎

The exact range results stated in Proposition 3.5, Corollary 3.8, Corollary 3.14 and Corollary 3.15 capture some generic supra-unitary (non-integer) rational parameters α\alpha with denominator b≥2b\geq 2. Specifically, we understand precisely the cases where α=k+1b\alpha=k+\frac{1}{b} and k≡uk\equiv u (mod bb) with u∈{0,1,b−1}u\in\{0,1,b-1\}, but, even in the small denominator cases, we are missing lots of the rational supra-unitary parameters. The result below is a counterpart to Proposition 3.5 which settles the exact ranges for all supra-unitary rational parameters with denominator 3.

Let s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}. Then

(ii) Let α=3​s+23\alpha=3s+\frac{2}{3}. Besides the general cases already settled above and performing ad-hoc calculations in the small denominators cases, such as in Proposition 3.5 or Proposition  3.16, identifying the exact Range⁡(fα)\Range(f_{\alpha}) for supra-unitary rational values of α\alpha seems to be a rather difficult task. It is not clear to these authors how to proceed in general for such parameters beyond the situations already addressed above. For example, our Wolfram Mathematica experimentations, see [4], are pretty convincing that the following statement should be true, but we are unable to prove it.

Conjecture 3.17.

For all b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-3.0mu\setminus\mkern-3.0mu\{1\}, all a∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketa\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket relatively prime to bb, and all s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} we have

Range⁡(fs​b−ab)=(s​\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracket)∪(s​\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracket−{1}).\Range\bigl(f_{sb-\frac{a}{b}}\bigr)=\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket\bigr)\cup\bigl(s\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket-\{1\}\bigr).

If indeed true, Conjecture 3.17 would generalize Corollary 3.15 which corresponds to a=b−1a=b-1. The following lemma is in the spirit of Lemma 3.9. The calculations are similar to the ones done there and left to the interested reader. We include it here since it may indicate a possible direction to deal with cases such as those in Conjecture 3.17.

Lemma 3.18.

Let b∈ℕ∖{1}b\in\mathbb{N}\mkern-1.0mu\setminus\mkern-2.0mu\{1\}, u∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbracketu\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket and a∈\llbracket​1,b−1​\rrbracketa\in\bigl\llbracket 1,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. Let n=b​t+r,n=bt+r, with t,r∈\llbracket​0,b−1​\rrbrackett,r\in\bigl\llbracket 0,b-1\bigr\rrbracket. Then

fs​b+u+ab​(n)=s​a​r−(s​b+u)​⌊a​rb⌋+⌊2​u​a​rb+a2​tb+a2​rb2⌋−⌊u​a​rb+a2​tb+ab​⌊a​rb⌋⌋.f_{sb+u+\frac{a}{b}}(n)=sar-(sb+u)\Big\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu\frac{ar}{b}\mkern-2.0mu\Big\rfloor+\bigg\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu\frac{2uar}{b}+\frac{a^{2}t}{b}+\frac{a^{2}r}{b^{2}}\mkern-2.0mu\bigg\rfloor-\bigg\lfloor\mkern-2.0mu\frac{uar}{b}+\frac{a^{2}t}{b}+\frac{a}{b}\Big\lfloor\frac{ar}{b}\Big\rfloor\mkern-2.0mu\bigg\rfloor.

4. Irrational parameters α\alpha

The goal of this section is to discuss a generalization of [3] and present several conjectures inspired by it and from extensive experimentations in Wolfram Mathematica, see [4].

4.2. Conjectures and partial results

By Proposition 2.1 we have

Range⁡(fα)⊆\llbracket​0,⌈α⌉​\rrbracket.\Range(f_{\alpha})\subseteq\bigl\llbracket 0,\lceil\alpha\rceil\bigr\rrbracket. (4.7)

Based on Wolfram Mathematica experimentation, see [4], we state the following

Conjecture 4.3.

For all positive irrational numbers α\alpha, we have

\llbracket​1,⌊α⌋​\rrbracket⊆Range⁡(fα).\bigl\llbracket 1,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\bigr\rrbracket\subseteq\Range(f_{\alpha}).

If Conjecture 4.3 is true, then we have the equality in Proposition 4.2.

Assuming Conjecture 4.3 holds, together with the inclusion in (4.7), suggests the following quadruplicity of the range result.

Proposition 4.4.

If Conjecture 4.3 is true, then for all positive irrational parameters α\alpha, one of the following equalities holds:

  1. (A)

    Range⁡(fα)=\llbracket​1,⌊α⌋​\rrbracket\displaystyle\Range(f_{\alpha})=\bigl\llbracket 1,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\bigr\rrbracket,

  2. (B)

    Range⁡(fα)=\llbracket​0,⌊α⌋​\rrbracket\displaystyle\Range(f_{\alpha})=\bigl\llbracket 0,\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\bigr\rrbracket,

  3. (C)

    Range⁡(fα)=\llbracket​1,⌈α⌉​\rrbracket\displaystyle\Range(f_{\alpha})=\bigl\llbracket 1,\lceil\alpha\rceil\bigr\rrbracket,

  4. (D)

    Range⁡(fα)=\llbracket​0,⌈α⌉​\rrbracket\displaystyle\Range(f_{\alpha})=\bigl\llbracket 0,\lceil\alpha\rceil\bigr\rrbracket.

Proof.

The equality in (A) holds for all irrational parameters considered in Proposition 4.1. In particular, we have Range⁡(fφ)={1}\Range(f_{\varphi})=\{1\}.

The equality in (D) holds for π\pi and ee. We used Wolfram Mathematica to calculate

fπ​(1)=0,fπ​(2)=fπ​(3)=1,fπ​(4)=fπ​(5)=2,fπ​(6)=3,fπ​(7)=4,f_{\pi}(1)=0,\ f_{\pi}(2)=f_{\pi}(3)=1,\ f_{\pi}(4)=f_{\pi}(5)=2,\ f_{\pi}(6)=3,\ f_{\pi}(7)=4,

and

fe(7)=fe(10)=0,fe(2)=fe(3)=fe(5)=fe(6)=fe(9)=1,fe(1)=fe(4)=fe(8)=2,fe(11)=3.f_{e}(7)=f_{e}(10)=0,\ f_{e}(2)=f_{e}(3)=f_{e}(5)=f_{e}(6)=f_{e}(9)=1,\\ f_{e}(1)=f_{e}(4)=f_{e}(8)=2,\ f_{e}(11)=3.

The equality in (C) holds for α=2\alpha=\sqrt{2}. Indeed,

Range⁡(f2)={1,2}.\Range\bigl(f_{\sqrt{2}}\bigr)=\{1,2\}.

First, f2​(k)=kf_{\sqrt{2}}(k)=k for k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\}, so {1,2}⊆Range⁡(f2)\{1,2\}\subseteq\Range\bigl(f_{\sqrt{2}}\bigr). Next, fix n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and set m=⌊2​n⌋m=\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{2}\,n\bigr\rfloor. By the definition of the floor, m≤2​n<m+1m\leq\sqrt{2}\,n<m+1. Since 2​n\sqrt{2}\,n is irrational, in fact m<2​n<m+1m<\sqrt{2}\,n<m+1. Multiplying by 2\sqrt{2} gives

2​n−2<2​m<2​n,2n-\sqrt{2}<\sqrt{2}\,m<2n,

hence ⌊2​m⌋∈{2​n−2,2​n−1}\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{2}\,m\bigr\rfloor\in\{2n-2,2n-1\}. Therefore

f2​(n)=2​n−⌊2​⌊2​n⌋⌋=2​n−⌊2​m⌋∈{1,2}.f_{\sqrt{2}}(n)=2n-\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{2}\,\lfloor\sqrt{2}\,n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor=2n-\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{2}\,m\bigr\rfloor\in\{1,2\}.

Thus Range⁡(f2)⊆{1,2}\Range\bigl(f_{\sqrt{2}}\bigr)\subseteq\{1,2\}, which, together with the converse inclusion, yields Range⁡(f2)={1,2}\Range\bigl(f_{\sqrt{2}}\bigr)=\{1,2\}.

The equality in (B) holds for α=2+2\alpha=2+\sqrt{2}. That is,

Range⁡(f2+2)={0,1,2,3}.\Range\bigl(f_{2+\sqrt{2}}\bigr)=\{0,1,2,3\}.

The inclusion {0,1,2,3}⊆Range⁡(f2+2)\{0,1,2,3\}\subseteq\Range\bigl(f_{2+\sqrt{2}}\bigr) follows from the equalities

f2+2​(1)=1,f2+2​(2)=3,f2+2​(3)=0,f2+2​(4)=2.f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(1)=1,\ f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(2)=3,\ f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(3)=0,\ f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(4)=2.

To prove the converse inclusion we use the following two properties of the floor function. For every positive real number xx with r=⌊4​(x−⌊x⌋)⌋∈{0,1,2,3}r=\bigl\lfloor 4\bigl(x-\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr)\bigr\rfloor\in\{0,1,2,3\} we have

⌊4​x⌋=4​⌊x⌋+r.\lfloor 4x\rfloor=4\lfloor x\rfloor+r.

For all positive integers n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and all positive real numbers xx we have

n−⌊x⌋=⌈n−x⌉.n-\lfloor x\rfloor=\lceil n-x\rceil.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} be arbitrary. A straightforward calculation shows that

f2+2​(n)=2​n+⌊4​2​n⌋−2​⌊2​n⌋−⌊2​2​n+2​⌊2​n⌋⌋.f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(n)=2n+\bigl\lfloor 4\sqrt{2}n\bigr\rfloor-2\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{2}n\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor 2\sqrt{2}n+\sqrt{2}\lfloor\sqrt{2}n\rfloor\bigr\rfloor.

m+r4\displaystyle m+\frac{r}{4} <2​n<m+r+14,\displaystyle<\sqrt{2}n<m+\frac{r+1}{4},
and, equivalently,

Considering the extreme cases for r∈{0,1,2,3}r\in\{0,1,2,3\}, that is r=0r=0 on the left-hand side and r=3r=3 on the right-hand side, we get the following open interval membership for ww:

w∈(−12,32+2).w\in\left(\mkern-3.0mu-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}+\sqrt{2}\right).

Consequently,

f2+2​(n)=⌈w⌉∈{0,1,2,3}.f_{2+\sqrt{2}}(n)=\lceil w\rceil\in\{0,1,2,3\}.

Since n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} was arbitrary, this proves Range⁡(f2+2)⊆{0,1,2,3}\Range\bigl(f_{2+\sqrt{2}}\bigr)\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}, and completes the proof. ∎

The conjectured statements in Proposition 4.4 account for the seemingly deep differences among positive irrational numbers. It would be interesting to explore these differences further. We state two more conjectures.

Conjecture 4.5.

For all irrational numbers α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) we have

Range⁡(fα)={0,1}.\Range(f_{\alpha})=\{0,1\}.

That is, all irrational α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) satisfy the equality in item (D) in Proposition 4.4.

Remark 4.1.

By Corollary 2.2, the preceding conjecture is equivalent to 1∈Range⁡(fα)1\in\Range(f_{\alpha}), which in turn is equivalent to the following statement: For every x>1x>1 there exists k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that

⌊x⁡⌈x​k⌉⌋≥⌈x2​k⌉.\bigl\lfloor x\lceil xk\rceil\bigr\rfloor\geq\bigl\lceil x^{2}k\bigr\rceil.

While Conjecture 4.5 was formulated based on experiments in Wolfram Mathematica, we now aim to provide some partial rigorous evidence in support of its validity.

Our first observation is that Conjecture 4.5 holds for all sub-unitary numbers α\alpha in some right-neighborhood of a square-root rational. We first set some notation. Let k,n∈ℕk,n\in\mathbb{N} be such that k<nk<n and assume that k/n\sqrt{k/n} is irrational. In this case, we call k/n\sqrt{k/n} a square-root rational, and denote it by sk,ns_{k,n}. With k,nk,n as above, we also write

ϵk,n=1n​min⁡{⌈k​n⌉−k​n,k​n−⌊k​n⌋}>0.\epsilon_{k,n}=\frac{1}{n}\min\left\{\bigl\lceil\sqrt{kn}\bigr\rceil-\sqrt{kn},\sqrt{kn}-\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{kn}\bigr\rfloor\right\}>0.
Proposition 4.6.

Let k,n∈ℕk,n\in\mathbb{N} be such that k<nk<n and sk,ns_{k,n} irrational. If α∈[sk,n,sk,n+ϵk,n)\alpha\in[s_{k,n},s_{k,n}+\epsilon_{k,n}), then fα​(n)=1f_{\alpha}(n)=1.

Proof.

Let x,y∈ℝx,y\in\mathbb{R}. The following three statements follow from the definitions of the floor and ceiling function:

⌊x⌋<y⇔⌊x⌋<⌈y⌉⇔x<⌈y⌉\lfloor x\rfloor<y\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\lfloor x\rfloor<\lceil y\rceil\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x<\lceil y\rceil

Let k,n∈ℕk,n\in\mathbb{N} be such that k<nk<n and assume that sk,n=k/ns_{k,n}=\sqrt{k/n} is irrational. Notice that sk,ns_{k,n} is irrational if and only if k​n\sqrt{kn} is irrational. To evaluate fsk,n​(n)f_{s_{k,n}}(n) we calculate

⌊(kn)2​n⌋=k,\left\lfloor\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\right)^{2}n\right\rfloor=k,

and estimate

⌊kn​⌊kn​n⌋⌋=⌊kn​⌊k​n⌋⌋<kn​⌊k​n⌋<kn​k​n=k.\Biggl\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\biggl\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\,n\biggr\rfloor\Biggr\rfloor=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{kn}\bigr\rfloor\right\rfloor<\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{kn}\bigr\rfloor<\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\sqrt{kn}=k.

Therefore fsk,n​(n)=1f_{s_{k,n}}(n)=1.

Let xx be a nonnegative real number such that x<ϵk,nx<\epsilon_{k,n}. In particular,

The only positive irrational number α\alpha for which the function fαf_{\alpha} is constant that we encountered in our explorations is α=φ\alpha=\varphi, the golden ratio. Therefore we conjecture:

Conjecture 4.7.

For all positive irrational α\alpha we have

Range(fα)={1}⇔α=φ.\Range(f_{\alpha})=\{1\}\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\alpha=\varphi.
Remark 4.2.

We disprove the following invariance conjecture: For all irrational α>1\alpha>1 and all p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, if Range⁡(fα)\Range(f_{\alpha}) satisfies the equality in item (X), where X ∈\in {\{A, B, C, D}\}, then Range⁡(fp​α)\Range(f_{p\alpha}) would also satisfy the same equality.

To disprove this conjecture, consider α=1+1/2\alpha=1+1/\sqrt{2} and calculate

fα​(1)=1,fα​(2)=0,fα​(7)=2.f_{\alpha}(1)=1,\quad f_{\alpha}(2)=0,\quad f_{\alpha}(7)=2.

Since ⌈α⌉=2\lceil\alpha\rceil=2, by Proposition 2.1 we have Range⁡(fα)={0,1,2}\Range(f_{\alpha})=\{0,1,2\}. Hence, α=1+1/2\alpha=1+1/\sqrt{2} satisfies the equality in item (D) in Proposition 4.4. Notice that 2​α=2+22\alpha=2+\sqrt{2}. We proved in the proof of Proposition 4.4 that 2​α=2+22\alpha=2+\sqrt{2} satisfies the equality in item (B) in Proposition 4.4.

We conclude with a couple of remarks regarding variations of the function fαf_{\alpha} discussed here.

Remark 4.3.

Throughout this article, we worked with the domain of the function fαf_{\alpha} being the set of positive integers. Naturally, one may ask what happens if we consider the domain as being the set of negative integers. For this, we note that, since ⌈x⌉=−⌊−x⌋\lceil x\rceil=-\lfloor-x\rfloor, given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we have

fα​(−n)=−gα​(n),f_{\alpha}(-n)=-g_{\alpha}(n),

where now gα:ℕ→ℤ,gα​(n)=⌈α2​n⌉−⌈α⁡⌈α​n⌉⌉.g_{\alpha}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z},\,g_{\alpha}(n)=\bigl\lceil\alpha^{2}\,n\bigr\rceil-\bigl\lceil\alpha\lceil\alpha n\rceil\bigr\rceil. In other words, fα​(−ℕ)=−gα​(ℕ)f_{\alpha}(-\mathbb{N})=-g_{\alpha}(\mathbb{N}); the analysis of the Range⁡(gα)\Range(g_{\alpha}) will most likely be of a similar flavor to one we have seen for Range⁡(fα)\Range(f_{\alpha}).

Remark 4.4.

Finally, one may ask about negative parameters α\alpha. Note now that for α<0\alpha<0, we can write fα=h−αf_{\alpha}=h_{-\alpha} where, for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and β>0,\beta>0, we have denoted

hβ​(n)=⌊β2​n⌋−⌊β⁡⌈β​n⌉⌋.h_{\beta}(n)=\bigl\lfloor\beta^{2}\,n\bigr\rfloor-\bigl\lfloor\beta\lceil\beta n\rceil\bigr\rfloor.

This is yet another variation on the function fαf_{\alpha}. There are a few other such variants, obtained by appropriately interchanging the floor and ceiling operations in the definition of fαf_{\alpha}. The analysis of their ranges is left to the interested reader.
